About 1.5 billion years ago, volcanic calderas
covered a section of Missouri in what is now southeastern
Missouri. These calderas formed as a result of molten
rock (magma) and gas squeezing up through underlying
chambers and causing a buildup of pressure just beneath
the surface rock. When enough pressure mounted, most
of the magma blasted through the rock, carving out
miles-wide craters. In the aftermath, the small amounts
of magma left behind in the chambers began cooling into
granite rock. When shards of surface rock and volcanic
ash tumbled into the newly exposed chambers, covering
the cooling magma with a layer thousands of feet thick.
Marina pointed toward the line of pink granite
boulders on the hill in front of us. She explained that, as
the years passed, the overlying layer of rock would of
eroded to reveal the granite. Wind and water rounded
the jagged edges of the blocks and polished this into
these boulders. In time, the constant cycle of uplift and
erosion would expose more underlying granite blocks—
